title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes

abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. Not applicable.

title: A new task of sustained attention: investigating the role of ADHD symptoms and response time variability in a task requiring children and adolescents to wait

abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

analysis.discussion: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. The findings conceptualize learning with GenAI as adaptive human-AI partnership. Metacognition supports goal setting, monitoring of AI contributions, evaluation, and subsequent regulation. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. The central challenge for GenAI-enhanced foreign language education is not how much learning can be delegated to AI, but how AI can be integrated while preserving and strengthening learners' capacity to think, evaluate, regulate, and act independently.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent reviewer or coder verification, which may have introduced selection or interpretive bias despite the use of a structured coding framework and documented screening decisions. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, reflecting the theory-building focus and methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. The database coverage also represents a limitation. Although Web of Science and Scopus provided broad multidisciplinary coverage, PsycINFO and ERIC were not searched. Future reviews should incorporate education and psychology-specific databases to broaden coverage and reduce potential database-related selection bias. Overall, the MTC Framework should be viewed as a theory-generating account that requires further empirical validation. The evidence also relied substantially on self-reports, interviews, surveys, and relatively short-term interventions. Although these approaches provide valuable insights into learners' perceptions and experiences, they may not fully capture how metacognitive regulation, trust calibration, and cognitive redistribution unfold during actual learner-AI interaction. Future research should therefore incorporate more longitudinal and process-sensitive approaches, including interaction logs, prompt histories, revision records, think-aloud protocols, and screen-based observation. Further research should examine how learner proficiency, prior AI experience, AI literacy, metacognitive ability, task complexity, instructional design, and teacher mediation shape MTC processes. In particular, the proposed framework requires empirical testing. Longitudinal, experimental, and mixed-methods research could examine whether metacognitive engagement is associated with trust calibration, whether calibrated reliance is associated with particular forms of co-regulation, and whether these processes are subsequently related to language-learning and psychological outcomes.

title: Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education
preview: A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. abstract_text:
A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments.
 
Implications for practice or policy:

University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability.
Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development.
Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks.
Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives.
Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Objective: Deficits in attention have been linked to poorer performance on executive functioning tasks, particularly those requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility. While continuous performance tests are commonly used to assess sustained attention, their relationship to error based executive outcomes under increased task demand in pediatric clinical populations remains incompletely characterized. This study examined whether performance on a relatively low demand task of sustained attention, the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test–Third Edition (CPT-3), predicts performance on a higher demand executive task, the Delis–Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS) Color Word Interference Test (CW). Method/Data Selection: Data were obtained from a mixed clinical sample of 213 children and adolescents ages 8–17 years (M = 11.7, SD = 2.8; 47.8% male, 52.2% female) evaluated in an outpatient private practice neuropsychology clinic. Participants completed the CPT-3 and D-KEFS CW as part of individualized comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. Multivariate regression analyses examined whether CPT-3 subscales predicted performance on D-KEFS CW conditions. Results/Data Synthesis: The overall model significantly predicted D-KEFS Inhibition Error scores (R2 = .12, adjusted R2 = .08, F(9, 198) = 3.02, p = .002) and D-KEFS Inhibition/Switching Error scores (R2 = .17, adjusted R2 = .13, F(9, 198) = 4.56, p &lt; .001). CPT-3 reaction time–based indices accounted for the majority of explained variance across both error outcomes. Conclusions: Performance on a sustained attention task was associated with error based executive performance requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility in this pediatric clinical sample. Faster response speed and higher variability in response speed may be linked more impulsive verbal responding, resulting in higher errors on a cognitively demanding task.

title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by …
abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by treating the educational effect of GenAI not as a property of the tool but as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine. Integrating research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and self-regulated learning, the framework holds that offloading augments learning when it discharges operations peripheral to the current learning goal, and risks erosion, whether of acquisition or of maintenance, when it bypasses the processing constitutive of that goal, unless the learner substantively processes the output or later reconstructs it. It supplies criteria for locating operations along a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum, specifies the comparison condition against which augmentation and erosion are defined, and states seven conditioned, testable propositions, each illustrated with a common example and paired with supporting and challenging patterns. On this basis, offloading regulation is proposed as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components: a competence comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization, enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners’ goals and motivation. The article closes with an intervention research program, a measurement strategy that triangulates interaction logs with process measures, and equity implications, using STEM learning as a strategically revealing case.

title: Trust in Generative AI and Critical Thinking Among College Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis Based on Perceived Usefulness, Cognitive Offloading, and AI Self-Efficacy
preview: This study examines how college students’ trust in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is associated with critical thinking engagement in GenAI-supported learning through multiple psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Distributed Cognition Theory (DCT), we propose and test a structural model including five constructs: trust in AI, perceived usefulness, cognitive offloading, AI self-efficacy, and critical think…
abstract_text: This study examines how college students’ trust in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is associated with critical thinking engagement in GenAI-supported learning through multiple psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Distributed Cognition Theory (DCT), we propose and test a structural model including five constructs: trust in AI, perceived usefulness, cognitive offloading, AI self-efficacy, and critical thinking. Drawing on survey data from a convenience sample of college students who engaged in learning activities using GenAI tools (e.g., ChatGPT), we assessed hypothesized relationships using structural equation modeling (SEM). The results show that trust in AI is positively associated with perceived usefulness and AI self-efficacy, and both constructs are positively associated with critical thinking. In contrast, cognitive offloading is negatively associated with critical thinking, indicating a potential constraining pathway through which stronger reliance on GenAI may be associated with lower engagement in higher-order thinking. Overall, the findings suggest that trust in GenAI is linked to critical thinking through both supportive and constraining pathways. This study extends DCT in GenAI-supported learning by showing that trust in AI is not uniformly beneficial. The findings highlight the importance of educational approaches that cultivate students’ efficacy beliefs and strategic use of GenAI while discouraging overreliance that reduces cognitive engagement.

abstract_text: This study examines how undergraduate students integrate generative AI tools into home exams and how these practices relate to self-regulated learning (SRL) and academic performance. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed exam responses, self-reports, and performance data from 891 students enrolled in BA-level qualitative methodology courses (2023–2024). Students were permitted to use AI if they disclosed their usage. Three modes of AI engagement were identified: instrumental (task completion with minimal evaluation), ideational (idea generation and selective integration), and reflective (critical evaluation and feedback-driven refinement). At a general level, AI use was associated with increased efficiency and somewhat higher performance than non-use. However, these aggregate patterns masked substantial variation across modes of use. Instrumental use was associated with weaker performance in some tasks, including definition tasks where reliance on generic AI-generated responses did not align with course-specific criteria. In contrast, reflective engagement with AI was associated with stronger and more consistent performance. Interpreted through an SRL framework, these findings suggest that outcomes of AI use depend on how students regulate its use. Rather than uniformly supporting or undermining learning, AI appears to amplify differences in students’ self-regulatory capacities. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing skills for critical and reflective engagement with AI.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in the "Introduction to Qualitative Methods" course offered to undergraduate students in the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Eastern Finland. The compulsory course is taken in the second or third year by students in social sciences, health and social management, business, geography, and open university. Instruction and assessment were conducted in Finnish (quotes are translated into English). The dataset is based on a home exam consisting of three tasks. The first task asked students to define a key concept in qualitative research. To receive the maximum score, students had to provide an accurate definition, elaborate on it using course materials, and contextualize it within qualitative research. The second task assessed students' ability to apply a qualitative analysis method to a short dataset. High-scoring responses included an appropriate research question, a description of the selected method, a clear account of the analytical process (coding and theme development), and a coherent interpretation of findings. The third task required students to evaluate the methodological and ethical aspects of a research setting. Full credit required identifying strengths and limitations in relation to research questions, data collection, analysis, and ethics. Emphasis was placed on internal consistency, that is, recognizing how individual design choices combine into a coherent qualitative approach. The study used authentic course data, meaning that assessment was conducted by the course instructor as part of the normal course process, and the research began only after grading had been completed. Consequently, inter-rater reliability was not calculated. However, the use of a structured rubric and the re-evaluation of a subset of responses supported consistency in grading. Students received information about the research via the course page and email, and those who declined participation were excluded. The study complied with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, 2016/679) and the Finnish Data Protection Act (1050/2018). All data were pseudonymized prior to analysis. The dataset includes home exam materials from 413 students in 2023 and 478 students in 2024 (total N = 891). We used five types of data: exam answers, platform log data, exam results, self-reported AI use, and course feedback (Table 1 ). Each dataset served a distinct role within a mixed-methods design. Exam answers, self-reports, and feedback formed the basis for qualitative analysis of AI use, while performance (points and grades) and log data (completion time) supported quantitative analysis of outcomes and efficiency. After course completion, we compiled all exam data into a spreadsheet containing exam year, submission time, task scores, total points, final grade, and self-reported AI use. Anonymous course feedback was not linked to individual students and was analyzed separately. The qualitative analysis focused on exams in which students reported AI use. We conducted a thematic analysis to identify patterns in AI use (Braun & Clarke, 2021) . The coding proceeded in four steps: 1) inductive coding of self-reports, 2) identification of recurring patterns, 3) deductive coding of exam responses with cross-validation to self-reports based on created criteria, and 4) deductive coding of course feedback. We identified three modes of AI use: instrumental, ideational, and reflective. In self-reports students described instrumental use as editing or directly adapting AI-generated text, ideational use as using AI for idea generation, and reflective use as evaluating their writing with AI tools. The first author conducted the initial inductive coding, after which the third author reviewed coding. Rather than conducting independent blind coding, the review process focused on evaluating the conceptual coherence of the categories, discussing ambiguous cases, and refining category boundaries. Particular attention was given to distinctions between instrumental and ideational use, which were less clearly differentiated than reflective use. Specifically, some students used AI primarily for improving language, grammar, or structure while leaving the substantive content largely unchanged. After discussion, these cases were classified as instrumental use because AI functioned mainly as an editing tool rather than as a source of ideas or reflective feedback. Because many self-reports were brief, we developed additional classification criteria (typical indicators) to support the following deductive coding. To refine these criteria, we compared a sample of student responses from each mode with example answers generated by ChatGPT 3.5, which was used by 85% of the students, and with established indicators of AI-generated text (Simon, 2023) . We focused on three dimensions: 1) content (superficial analysis, contextual misalignment, generic responses and factual inconsistencies in relation to course materials), 2) structure (formulaic organization, weak logical connections, mechanical use of transitions, and similar structural patterns across task types), and 3) style (overly formal tone, overly polished appearance, generic or vague wording, repetitiveness, lack of personal voice). Instrumental use was coded when AI-generated content formed the primary basis of the response with minimal modification. Ideational use was coded when AI outputs were selectively integrated into student-authored text. Reflective use was coded when AI was used primarily to refine students' own responses. In ambiguous cases, classification was based on the dominant pattern across content, structure, and style indicators. Together, we used these steps to develop the coding scheme (Appendix 1). In the final stage of qualitative analysis, by using a coding scheme, we deductively coded exam responses and open-ended course feedback. We then added AI modes to the spreadsheet, coding each exam response as non-use, instrumental, ideational, or reflective. Because AI use varied across tasks (Table 2 ), analyses were conducted at the task level, with each task treated as an independent observation. Where aggregated performance measures were used, these were calculated by combining task-level scores. We then conducted quantitative analysis by linking modes of AI use to performance (points and grades) and efficiency (completion time). First, the quantitative analysis focused on differences in results between students who used AI and those who did not. The differences were studied using a non-parametric U test due to unequal group sizes and non-normal distribution of scores. To study the possible differences in exam results between students in different modes of AI, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used. The quantitative part of the study was conducted using Jamovi software. Within the SRL framework, the decision to use AI as a resource (and for which tasks) was interpreted as part of the forethought phase. Exam performance reflected the performance phase, and self-reports represented selfreflection. Course feedback further illuminated metacognitive reflections and motivational and emotional aspects across all phases. At the same time, reporting requirements encouraged students to monitor and reflect on their own practices. We present
analysis.discussion: Our findings suggest a gradual normalization of AI use in academic settings, reflected in increased uptake and more positive attitudes, aligning with prior research indicating generally neutral or positive student perceptions of AI in education (Ardelean & Edit, 2023; Jinchuña Huallpa et al., 2023) . However, ethical concerns persisted, particularly regarding whether AI-assisted exam work constitutes genuine learning. Similar student concerns have been identified in contexts AI use may compromise fairness and skill development (Chaudhry et al., 2023) . Overall, the findings challenge the notion of students as uniform adopters of AI. Instead, attitudes and emotions toward AI differ, shaping how and whether students use LLMs in academic tasks. This variation underlines the need for more nuanced, context-sensitive accounts of AI use in authentic learning situations. This study shows that students' use of AI in academic tasks is not uniform but varies in meaningful ways. We identified three modes of AI use-instrumental, ideational, and reflective-and found that these are associated with different levels of engagement and performance. Students who engaged more evaluatively with AI tended to demonstrate stronger and more consistent outcomes, while more instrumental use was sometimes associated with weaker performance, especially in tasks requiring contextualization and critical interpretation. Taken together, these findings indicate that the role of AI in learning depends on how students use it. AI is not inherently beneficial or harmful; rather, its effects depend on how students regulate its use. In this sense, AI makes students' self-regulatory capacities more visible and potentially more consequential. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing the skills needed to use AI thoughtfully and critically, so that it contributes to meaningful learning rather than mere task completion.
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, the data were collected during the early stages of widespread generative AI adoption, when many students were still experimenting with the technology. As a result, the proposed categorization of AI use should be considered an initial framework, open to further refinement. In addition, the study was conducted in the context of home exams, which represent a specific assessment setting. Comparisons to more complex academic tasks, such as thesis writing, should therefore be made with caution, as students may employ multiple AI strategies across extended projects and use a wider range of tools. Second, the study is based on naturally occurring data without experimental control. Consequently, self-regulated learning processes were inferred rather than directly measured. The analysis relies primarily on self-reports, which varied in detail and did not include prompts, limiting insight into actual AI interactions. This may have affected the classification of AI use, particularly in distinguishing between ideational and reflective modes. In addition, it is possible that some students did not disclose their AI use, which could lead to under-or overestimation of differences between groups. As AI models evolved rapidly during data collection (2023-2024), differences in tool capabilities may have influenced the effectiveness of certain usage strategies. And variation in exam tasks across sessions may also affect comparability, despite the use of a shared grading rubric. A further limitation concerns interpretation. As an observational and mainly qualitative study, the findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships. In particular, students who engaged in more evaluative or reflective forms of AI use may already have differed from others in terms of prior ability, motivation, or self-regulatory capacity. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether differences in performance are related to AI use itself or to underlying student characteristics. The study is also limited by its theoretical framing. Although selfregulated learning provided a useful framework for identifying differences in students' AI use, the aim was not to measure or validate SRL processes as such. Consequently, the findings primarily, and somewhat simplistically, draw attention to students' self-regulation in integrating AI as a learning resource. Alternative theoretical perspectives, such as deep learning or digital literacy, might have provided greater insight into the learning processes themselves or the critical skills required to use AI tools. Both of these aspects deserve further exploration. Thus, the study provides only partial access to students' learning processes. While self-reports and feedback offer useful insights, they do not capture students' internal motivations, planning strategies, or realtime decision-making. In particular, motivational factors such as task value, goal orientation, and self-efficacy were not directly measured, even though the findings suggest they play an important role in shaping AI use. Given the complexity of motivation as a research domain, future studies would benefit from employing methods specifically designed to capture these dimensions more systematically. The findings cannot be generalized statistically to all higher education contexts where students use generative AI for written assignments. The study is based on an authentic teaching situation, with all its inherent imperfections, and it began as a qualitative and conceptual process to which quantitative elements were added later on. The findings should therefore be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive. However, the consistency of the identified patterns across two academic years suggests that the distinction between instrumental, ideational, and reflective AI use may have relevance beyond the specific course examined here. Despite these limitations, the study highlights the complex and nonuniform role of AI in educational settings. Drawing on authentic assessment context, longitudinal design spanning two academic years, and triangulated data, the study provides a robust account of how students engage with AI in practice. The findings suggest that the pedagogical value of AI depends less on the tool itself and more on how students regulate its use within learning processes. The findings may inform educational decision-making in several ways. First, they suggest that educational interventions should focus not only on whether students use AI, but also on how they use it. Second, instruction on AI literacy should emphasize critical evaluation, adaptation, and reflection rather than task completion. Third, assessment practices may benefit from rewarding contextualization, critical thinking, and reflective engagement, which appear to distinguish higher-performing forms of AI use. Future research should examine how instructional approaches and targeted support can help students engage with AI in ways that sustain autonomy, critical thinking, and deep learning.

abstract_text: This study examined students’ AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, and ethical awareness following participation in a structured, AI-integrated classroom activity. The study also investigated the relationships among these constructs and examined whether perceived learning benefits mediate the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. In addition, the study explored whether students’ responses differed according to gender, prior AI experience, and frequency of AI use. The study involved 104 undergraduate students who participated in a hands-on classroom activity over two academic semesters. Students used generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, to prepare and deliver short lessons to their classmates, followed by discussions addressing responsible and ethical AI use. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, ethical awareness, and related aspects of students’ experiences. Overall, students reported positive perceptions of the learning experience. They strongly agreed that AI made learning easier and more enjoyable (M = 4.29), saved time on academic tasks (M = 4.27), and helped improve the quality of their work (M = 4.09). AI literacy was positively correlated with perceived learning benefits (r = 0.559, p .05). The findings suggest that students’ AI literacy is associated with greater perceived learning benefits and ethical awareness. Furthermore, the study examines the potential mediating role of perceived learning benefits in the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. These findings highlight the importance of structured, meaningful classroom activities that encourage students to actively engage with, evaluate, and take responsibility for AI-generated content rather than relying on AI outputs passively.

Direct association (X → Y): The direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant after accounting for Perceived Benefits (β = 0.165, p = .091). Indirect effect (X → M → Y): The indirect effect was statistically significant (Effect = 0.194, BootLLCI = 0.051, BootULCI = 0.361). Because the bootstrap confidence interval does not include zero, the results provide evidence consistent with an indirect mediation pathway. The results showed that after the AI activity, students had good AI literacy (M = 3.81), very good perceived benefits (M = 4.22), and good ethical awareness (M = 4.10). Students said that AI helped them save time (71.2%), improved their ability to solve problems (71.2%), and strengthened their critical thinking (62.5%). At the same time, some students worried about incorrect AI outputs (54.8%) and plagiarism (35.0%). This shows that students have a balanced and thoughtful view of AI tools. The statistical analysis also showed that students who had used AI before the activity had higher perceived benefits (p = .003) and higher ethical awareness (p = .005). However, gender and academic level did not make any difference in the results. Also, how often students used AI was linked to all three areas (p < .01). This means that using AI more often helps students build better skills and awareness.
analysis.discussion: The results indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness through Perceived Benefits, while the direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant. These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness may operate indirectly through Perceived Benefits. However, given the cross-sectional design, these findings are correlational and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal pathway. Higher levels of perceived AI Literacy were associated with higher Perceived Benefits, which were in turn associated with higher Ethical Awareness. The aim of this study was to analyze the influence of the class activity based on the application of generative AI on the AI literacy, learning benefits perceived by undergraduate students, and their ethical awareness. The findings have shown a statistically significant indirect effect of the AI literacy on the ethical awareness via the perception of learning benefits, as hypothesized in the proposed theory. This relationship is in line with-but does not prove-the possible process through which AI literacy is associated with the perception of the usefulness of AI, which is further associated with perceived learning benefits (savings in time, improvement in quality, pleasure) and, finally, with ethical awareness. This finding aligns with Self-Determination Theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000) . When students experience competence through perceived benefits, they are more likely to internalize responsible behaviors. It also supports Expectancy-Value Theory (Eccles and Wigfield, 2002) , where value beliefs (perceived benefits) mediate the relationship between competence beliefs (AI literacy) and behavioral outcomes (ethical awareness). Notably, the insignificant direct effect (β = 0.165, p = .091) together with the significant indirect effect suggests that AI literacy does not have a direct association with ethical awareness when learning gains are controlled for. This implies several important implications for teaching practice: instructors must not rely on the belief that the mere teaching of AI techniques fosters responsible conduct. Students must also experience and value the benefits of AI use.
analysis.limitations: • First, the sample (N = 104) came from only one university, and students were chosen based on convenience. This means the results may not apply to all students. • Second, the study used self-reported answers, which may not be completely accurate (common method bias; Podsakoff et al., 2003) because students might answer in a way they think looks good. • Third, there was no control group, so we cannot say for sure that the activity caused the results. • Fourth, the study measured outcomes right after the activity. We need follow-up studies to see if the gains in literacy, benefits, and awareness last over time, • Fifth, although the study included open-ended questions, a systematic qualitative analysis was not conducted. Therefore, the study should be characterized as predominantly quantitative, with qualitative data used for exploratory purposes only. Future research should employ rigorous qualitative methods such as thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) or in-depth interviews to capture richer insights into students' experiences, • Sixth, the study's findings are based on self-reported data, which may be subject to social desirability bias or inaccurate recall. Future studies should incorporate objective measures of student performance and AI interaction behaviors (Podsakoff et al., 2003) .

abstract_text: The call for papers for the 2025 PESA conference referenced our ‘increasingly pluralistic, post-truth, post-reality and divided world’ and the ‘existential problems’ that we face—noting climate change, AI, populism and the decline in ethical and reasoned discourse. The assumption contained in the call was that equipping young people with the ability to engage in reasoned deliberation is more pressing than ever before. And certainly, educating for critical thinking—thoughtfulness, coherence, rationality—is often held up as a silver bullet to heal our seemingly ailing and divided world. Perhaps rightly so. But here, I apply some critical thinking to the claim. Drawing on many years of involvement in teaching philosophy and ethics at the tertiary level, I reflect on what teaching critical thinking skills can, and cannot, achieve. I question the pervasive ‘crisis’ framing in education, suggesting that constant existential rhetoric can leave students anxious and less resilient and I argue for some guiding principles: teach students how to think, not what to think; and guard against ideological narrowing, ensuring critical thinking is genuinely open to diverse perspectives, including those that make us uncomfortable. Rather than a cure-all, critical thinking should be taught as a discipline grounded in humility, charity, and the courage to engage with difference. Its power lies not in solving every societal problem, but in equipping students to reason together in good faith—even when the stakes are existential.

analysis.methods: The study used a cross-sectional survey design. Convenience sampling was used to administer paper-and-pencil questionnaires to undergraduate students at universities in mainland China during the 2024–2025 academic year. After data screening for completeness and inattentive responding, 421 valid questionnaires were retained for analysis. Of these participants, 128 (30.4%) identified as male and 293 (69.6%) as female. The sample comprised 116 first-year (27.6%), 101 second-year (24.0%), 164 third-year (39.0%) and 40 fourth-year (9.5%) students, drawn from a range of disciplines. The sample size comfortably exceeds the minimum required for PLS-SEM with the present model complexity, satisfying both Cohen’s power conventions and the inverse-square-root rule ( Hair et al., 2021 ; Kock and Hadaya, 2018 ). All participation was voluntary and anonymous. Before completing the questionnaire, students were informed of the study purpose and the protections in place; they gave written informed consent and were assured that responses would be used solely for academic research and that they could withdraw at any time. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the authors’ institution and approved by the relevant Institutional Review Board. To reduce potential common method bias, the questionnaire was pilot-tested on 30 undergraduates not included in the final sample, items were arranged so that the predictor and criterion measures were separated, and procedural remedies recommended by Podsakoff et al. (2003) were applied (e.g., guaranteed anonymity, balanced item polarity, and clear instructions emphasising that there were no right or wrong answers). All scales were administered in Chinese; English-language scales were translated and back-translated by two bilingual researchers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer and the wording revised after a small-scale pilot. Items were rated on a five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) unless otherwise noted. Scale scores reported in Table 1 were calculated as the sum of the constituent items, with higher scores indicating higher levels of the construct; for the PLS-SEM measurement model, dimension and parcel scores were computed as item means (Section 3.3), which is immaterial for estimation because PLS-SEM standardises all indicators. Means, standard deviations and zero-order correlations. GenAI use was measured with the 17-item College Students’ Generative AI Use Survey developed by Li et al. (2024) . The instrument captures students’ use of GenAI across four typical scenarios identified through literature review and semi-structured interviews with undergraduates: course learning, research activities, daily life, and further-study and job seeking. Sample items include “I use generative AI to answer the questions my teachers ask in class”, “I use generative AI to assist me in selecting research questions”, “When I encounter difficulties in life (such as diet, financial management or social relationships), I turn to generative AI for help”, and “I ask generative AI to help me create or revise my résumé”. The scale has demonstrated acceptable reliability in prior Chinese university samples. The critical-thinking outcome was operationalised as self-reported critical analytical skills using the eight-item Critical Analytical Skills sub-scale of Hou et al.’s (2022) Chinese Critical Thinking Scale. The sub-scale assesses individuals’ perceived ability to systematically gather and analyse problem-relevant background information and evaluate its veracity. Sample items include “I prefer to follow a structured set of steps when solving problems”, “I often consider the views of my parents and elders when making decisions”, and “I make different decisions in different situations when faced with a problem”. The Chinese Critical Thinking Scale was developed and validated specifically for Chinese university samples and has demonstrated good psychometric properties; higher scores indicate stronger self-reported critical analytical skills. Following the item-to-construct balance approach ( Little et al., 2002 ), the eight items were aggregated into three parcels for use as indicators of the latent critical analytical skills construct. Specifically, the items were first ranked according to their standardised factor loadings, and relatively higher- and lower-loading items were systematically distributed across the three parcels to balance their relationships with the underlying construct. Parcel scores were calculated as the mean of their constituent items. The resulting three parcels, labelled CT Parcel 1, CT Parcel 2, and CT Parcel 3, were specified as reflective indicators of a single latent critical analytical skills construct. They therefore represent aggregated measurement indicators rather than theoretically distinct dimensions of critical thinking ( Little et al., 2002 ; Matsunaga, 2008 ). GenAI feedback literacy was assessed using the 39-item Generative AI Student Feedback Literacy Scale (GenAI-SFLS) developed and validated for Chinese college students by Cui et al. (2026) . The instrument is organised around four dimensions and nine specific factors: a cognitive dimension (feedback knowledge and feedback appreciation); a behavioural dimension (feedback prompting skills, feedback judgement and enaction of feedback); an affective dimension (emotional recognition, readiness to engage and commitment to change); and an ethical dimension (feedback ethics). The four-dimension architecture extends Carless and Boud’s (2018) general feedback-literacy framework to AI-mediated environments, where prompt engineering and ethical engagement become central to the construct ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Zhan and Yan, 2026 ). Reflective thinking was measured with the Reflective Thinking Scale (RTS) developed by Kember et al. (2000) , one of the most widely used instruments in this area; in the present study, the Chinese-context revised version validated by Fu and Hali (2025) for use with students in mainland Chinese universities was adopted. The RTS captures four dimensions on a continuum of reflection: habitual action, understanding, reflection and critical reflection, with habitual action representing the least reflective level and critical reflection the most advanced. A sample item is “I often re-appraise my experience so I can learn from it and improve for my next performance”. Items were rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = definitely disagree, 5 = definitely agree). The four-factor structure has shown good reliability and construct validity in Chinese university samples ( Fu and Hali, 2025 ; Kember et al., 2000 ). The analysis proceeded in two stages. The four-factor model best represented the underlying factor structure (χ 2 /df = 2.189; CFI = 0.731; TLI = 0.723; IFI = 0.732; RMSEA = 0.053), with all factor loadings statistically significant. GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking were significantly and positively inter-correlated (all p < 0.001). The pattern is consistent with the proposed model: GenAI use is most strongly correlated with feedback literacy, and feedback literacy and reflective thinking show the strongest associations with critical thinking, anticipating their roles as mediator and moderator. AVE values exceeded 0.60 ( Barclay et al., 1995 ), indicating adequate convergent validity. The square root of each construct’s AVE exceeded its correlations with the other constructs, satisfying the Fornell–Larcker criterion. Heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) ratios across all construct pairs (0.309, 0.514, 0.583, 0.315, 0.715 and 0.546) were well below the conservative 0.85 threshold ( Henseler et al., 2016 ), supporting discriminant validity. Following Chin’s (2009) recommendation, the structural model was estimated in SmartPLS 4.1.1.4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Path coefficients are reported in Table 4 . The total effect of GenAI use on critical thinking, equivalent to its estimate when modelled without the mediator, was also significant ( β = 0.257, t = 4.864, p < 0.001), supporting H1. analysis.discussion: This study set out to test a moderated mediation model linking generative artificial intelligence use to university students’ self-reported critical thinking, with GenAI feedback literacy as the mechanism and reflective thinking as a boundary condition. Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. Third, the model was conditional on reflective thinking: at low reflective thinking the link was direct and the indirect path was not significant, whereas at high reflective thinking the indirect path through feedback literacy strengthened and the direct path disappeared. Read together, these results are consistent with a dual-route interpretation of the inconsistent existing evidence on GenAI and critical thinking, in which the structure of the association is sensitive to learner disposition. Each finding warrants discussion. Before turning to each finding, one interpretive boundary should be made explicit. Critical thinking was measured with the critical analytical skills sub-scale of the Chinese Critical Thinking Scale, on which students rate their own habitual analytical behaviour. The outcome therefore represents self-reported critical analytical skills, not critical-thinking performance demonstrated on a task, a test or an expert-rated piece of work. Self-reports of this kind capture students’ perceptions of how they approach problems rather than the observed quality of their reasoning, and they share a method with the self-reported predictors. Accordingly, where we write that GenAI use, feedback literacy or reflective thinking “predicts” critical thinking, the claim is that these variables are associated with higher self-rated analytical skill in a cross-sectional model, not that they produce better critical-thinking performance. This boundary applies to every finding discussed below. Generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the cognitive infrastructure of higher education, and a settled empirical answer to whether its use is associated with stronger or weaker critical thinking has remained elusive. The present study reframes the question. In a cross-sectional sample of Chinese undergraduates, GenAI use was positively associated with self-reported critical analytical skills, but the association was largely indirect: it was carried by students’ capacity to interpret, judge and act on AI-generated feedback, and its structure depended on students’ reflective stance. At low reflective thinking the association was direct and modest; at high reflective thinking it ran through feedback literacy, yielding a stronger indirect association. If these associations reflect the hypothesised causal ordering, a question that longitudinal and experimental designs must settle, the cognitive dividend of GenAI is unlikely to come from access alone, and universities that pair AI integration with explicit feedback-literacy training and reflective pedagogical practises may be better placed to convert ubiquitous AI use into the analytical capacity that higher education is meant to cultivate. The moderated mediation model presented here offers a tractable framework for the next wave of empirical work on GenAI and higher-order cognition.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations bound the study’s claims. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. All variables were measured concurrently, so the mediation and moderated-mediation estimates describe patterns of association that are consistent with the hypothesised ordering but cannot establish it; reverse or reciprocal orderings (for example, students with stronger analytical skills making heavier or more sophisticated use of GenAI, or feedback literacy shaping use rather than the reverse) are equally compatible with the data. Although PLS-SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects and theoretically motivated path direction is well suited to estimating complex models, the findings should be replicated using longitudinal panel data or randomised intervention designs that track how GenAI use, feedback literacy and reflective thinking co-evolve over time. Second, the sample is drawn from Chinese universities and is skewed female (69.6%); cross-cultural and gender-balanced replications are needed to assess generalisability across educational systems with different assessment cultures and AI-policy environments. Third, all measures are self-reported, and the outcome in particular represents self-reported critical analytical skills rather than demonstrated critical-thinking performance. Although the study’s common-method-bias diagnostics did not flag a serious problem, behavioural and performance-based measures of critical thinking and feedback engagement (e.g., analyses of think-aloud protocols, log data from AI interactions, expert ratings of student work) would strengthen inference ( Fan et al., 2025 ). Fourth, critical thinking was operationalised through the analytical-skills sub-scale of a Chinese instrument; future studies could examine the model with broader operationalisations covering inference, evaluation, explanation and self-regulation ( Facione, 2011 ) and across disciplines, since GenAI’s affordances and risks may differ between, say, the humanities and STEM. Relatedly, the dual-route interpretation in this study rests on the pattern of moderation, not on direct observation of cognitive processing; the study did not measure whether students engaged with GenAI outputs shallowly or deeply, and process-tracing methods such as interaction logs, think-aloud protocols or eye-tracking are needed to test the proposed routes directly. Fifth, the incremental fit indices of the item-level measurement model fell below conventional thresholds, as is common with long instruments such as the 39-item GenAI-SFLS ( Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ); future work could refine the GenAI-SFLS for shorter administration without losing dimensional coverage. Finally, GenAI tools are evolving rapidly, and the empirical model captures a snapshot of usage patterns at a given moment; tracking the moderated mediation structure across model generations and modalities (text, voice, multimodal agents) is an important agenda for the field.

title: From digital companionship to capability building: reframing conversational artificial intelligence and older adults' psychological wellbeing in active aging
preview: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emot…
abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emotional support. While this perspective captures important affective outcomes, it offers a limited account of the developmental processes through which AI engagement may influence psychological wellbeing in aging populations. This conceptual analysis proposes a shift from a companionship-oriented paradigm to a capability-building perspective grounded in the Capability Approach. It argues that the primary value of conversational AI lies not in its ability to substitute social interaction, but in its potential to expand older adults' cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capabilities. Building on this argument, this paper develops an AI-Augmented Active Aging Framework that explains how conversational AI affordances, responsiveness, personalization, accessibility, and availability, interact with personal, social, environmental, and system-level conversion factors. Under supportive conditions, these affordances may facilitate cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capability formation, thereby supporting autonomy, competence, social integration, and active aging. Under adverse conditions, however, conversational AI may contribute to capability erosion through over-reliance, cognitive offloading, reduced human contact, or diminished autonomous judgment. The framework therefore emphasizes heterogeneous and conditional outcomes rather than assuming uniform benefits across older adults.

abstract_text: The importance of critical thinking when using generative AI in personal, professional, and educational contexts is widely acknowledged by scholars, educators, and politicians. There are contradictory hypotheses regarding the influence of AI on critical thinking, and research thus far has produced mixed results. In this paper, we present a critical scoping review of 80 research papers from Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) that study critical thinking with or about AI, focusing on how “critical thinking” is defined, measured, and how the papers claim critical thinking to be influenced by AI, according to current HCI research. Our findings demonstrate that critical thinking is rarely defined in HCI research about AI, and there are fundamental construct and criterion validity challenges in this line of research. We present a research agenda for more theory-grounded empirical research in critical thinking with or about AI, based on cognitive-psychological, philosophical, or educational research traditions.
